text: A resource group is where every Azure resource actually lives, and understanding what it does - and doesn't do - is the second piece of the governance picture after subscriptions and management groups. It sounds like a simple folder, but the way it behaves has real consequences the first time you delete one.

az group create --name rg-prod-eastus-web --location eastus creates a container; the location you give it is just where its own metadata is stored, not where every resource inside has to live. az group delete removes the group and, critically, everything inside it at once - there's no separate step to empty it first, which is exactly why resource group boundaries deserve real thought before you deploy into one.

Here's the detail that ties the whole platform together: the Azure Portal, Azure CLI, Azure PowerShell, and every ARM template all do the same thing underneath - they send a request to the Azure Resource Manager API. ARM is the single control plane every Azure action passes through, no matter which tool you clicked or typed, and it's also where RBAC and policy actually get checked before anything happens.

An ARM template is a JSON file - or its cleaner, more readable cousin, Bicep - that declares what you want deployed, rather than the step-by-step commands to build it. ARM reads the template, compares it to what's already running, and only changes what's actually different. Submit the same template twice and the second run makes no changes at all, which is what makes templates safe to re-run as part of a repeatable deployment process.

Because resources in a resource group share a lifecycle, the group is also where you apply protection against accidents: az lock create with --lock-type CanNotDelete stops anyone from deleting the group, or anything in it, until the lock itself is explicitly removed - a safety net worth setting on anything running in production, independent of whatever delete permissions someone's RBAC role happens to grant them.

Resource groups and ARM are the mechanics of where resources live and how they actually get deployed. Next: how to name and place those resources - Azure regions, paired regions for disaster recovery, and a naming convention that keeps a growing resource list readable six months from now.
